name: Rice water rinse

card.summary: A starchy, often fermented rice soak used as a hair rinse; long tradition, thin research, and buildup reported on some hair types.
card.note: Growth claims are anecdotal; protein or starch buildup can leave hair stiff or brittle.

quick.overview:
Rice water rinse means pouring the liquid from soaked, rinsed or boiled rice, often fermented, over hair after shampoo. It has a long traditional reputation in parts of Asia and is popular today for claimed strength, shine and length.

AI-generated Grokipedia reports no strong evidence that it lengthens hair, and says the small trials that exist mostly studied rice bran products.
quick.mechanism: Believers credit inositol, amino acids and starch, which are said to coat or enter the shaft, reducing friction and breakage. Fermentation adds acidity. The mechanisms are proposed rather than confirmed for rice water.
quick.risks: Reported downsides include protein or starch buildup causing dryness, stiffness and brittleness, especially in curly hair. Rice can carry arsenic, a concern mainly for ingestion. Spoiled rice water is described as something to discard.

lead: A rice water rinse is a hair treatment in which the starchy liquid left from soaking, rinsing or boiling rice, often fermented for a day or two, is applied to the hair and scalp after shampooing. People use it to get smoother, shinier, stronger-feeling hair that breaks less, and many hope it helps hair reach greater length.[1]

Wikipedia states that women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia have reportedly used rice water on their hair for centuries, and that women in Japan's Heian period (794-1185) were reportedly able to keep very long, healthy hair by washing it in rice water.[2] The best-known modern reference is the Yao women of Huangluo, China, whose long hair is attributed by themselves and by popular media to regular fermented rice rinses.[1]

Proponents credit amino acids and inositol, a carbohydrate, for reduced friction, better elasticity and less breakage. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that strong scientific evidence for faster growth or added length is lacking and that claims are largely anecdotal.[1] The rinse appears in K-beauty hair routines and in hair-growth discussions on forums, where one T Nation thread describes people being 'all over' fermented rice water alongside minoxidil.[3]

Researchers have looked at rice water mainly through its social-media presence. Dermatology journals have published a cross-sectional analysis of rice water for hair and skin on TikTok (2025) and a Cutis review of the evidence behind topical hair-loss remedies popularised on TikTok, which lists rice water alongside rosemary oil, onion juice and garlic gel (2023).[7][8]

chain: Rice-water rinse coats the hair after shampooing
Starch and inositol are said to cut friction and add strength
Smoother, shinier hair that breaks less and holds length
angle.text: The appearance payoff users describe is shinier, softer, less tangled hair that snaps less, so it looks longer and fuller over time. Fermented versions are favoured by people who say the slightly acidic liquid leaves hair smoother.[1]

infobox: About 12 to 48 hours at room temperature[1]

paras: Rice water is a starchy, milky liquid obtained by soaking, rinsing or boiling rice. Grokipedia distinguishes plain rice water, which is the runoff from rinsing uncooked rice, fermented rice water left at room temperature for roughly 12 to 48 hours, and boiled rice water drained after cooking.[1] Wikipedia describes rice water more generally as a starch suspension made by draining boiled rice or boiling rice until it dissolves.[2]

For hair, Grokipedia describes a typical routine as shampooing, pouring the liquid over scalp and strands, massaging it in, leaving it for about 20 minutes and rinsing with warm water, with some people mixing it into masks with oils or leaving it on longer.[1] The page gives plain rice water a pH of about 5.5 to 7 and fermented versions about 4 to 5, and says fermentation acidifies the liquid, though it does not tie the pH to a measured hair outcome.[1]

Wikipedia notes that women in various Asian regions, including China, Japan and Southeast Asia, have applied rice water as a hair treatment for hundreds of years, and dates the Japanese use to the Heian period (794-1185 CE), when women reportedly had floor-length hair kept healthy by washing in it.[2] The same article records long use of rice water as a food, including for digestive illness and diarrhoea, citing a 1981 Lancet report on infantile gastroenteritis and a 1992 BMJ meta-analysis of rice-based rehydration solutions.[2]

Grokipedia places rice water in Ayurvedic practice, where it appears under the name tandulodaka, in a 16th-century Chinese materia medica, and in European medicine by the 18th century as a bland diet for diarrhoea; it also notes use in Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand.[1] The Yao women of Huangluo attribute their exceptionally long hair to regular fermented rice-water rinses, a story the same source describes as anecdotal that has spread through media and into K-beauty routines.[1]

Proponents attribute benefits to several components. Inositol is said to penetrate the hair shaft, help repair damage, increase elasticity and reduce surface friction; amino acids are said to strengthen hair and improve smoothness; and starches and lipids are credited with moisture retention and shine.[1] Grokipedia states that these mechanisms have not been established for rice water specifically.[1]

Rice water is also used on skin, where Grokipedia reports use as a toner, bath additive and mask, with ferulic acid and fermentation-derived lactic acid cited as the active ingredients; the page itself cautions that several of its citations do not clearly match its claims.[1]

sections.h: Doctrines and mechanisms as described by proponents
paras: Proponents describe rice water as a leave-in or short-contact conditioner. Inositol, amino acids and starch are the ingredients most often named, and the stated outcome is a smoother cuticle, less friction between strands and less snapping during combing, so that hair retains length it would otherwise lose.[1] The fermented form is favoured by users who value its lower pH, which they associate with a flatter cuticle and more shine.[1]

A 2024 systematic review of rice-washed water in the Journal of Food Science and Technology surveyed its processing, nutrient content, use in growing edible fungi and plants, and traditional roles in Ayurveda, food and cosmetics. Its authors note that little research exists and that the traditional uses still need scientific validation.[8]

Grokipedia reports that protein or starch buildup may cause dryness, stiffness or brittleness, especially in curly or coily hair, and that low-porosity hair may coat and frizz while high-porosity hair may absorb too much protein and feel straw-like.[1] The page suggests heavily diluted, infrequent use and stopping if hair becomes brittle.[1]

It adds that room-temperature fermentation can encourage bacterial growth and that rice can accumulate inorganic arsenic, a concern it frames mainly for internal consumption; rare allergic reactions to rice are also noted.[1]

No studies found of rice water rinses on hair in people. Grokipedia says a 2022 systematic review reported possible benefits for hair strength and breakage over 8 to 12 weeks, but that it mainly covered rice bran extracts and related products rather than rice water, and that the trials had fewer than 50 participants each.[1] That summary comes from an AI-generated source rather than a primary study.

Published work on fermented rice water in other settings includes food-science research on using fermented washed rice water in a Korean rice cake,[4] and laboratory and animal studies of probiotic strains from fermented rice water,[5][6] none of which tested hair outcomes.

Systematic work on the broader category exists: the 2024 review of rice-washed water found the evidence base for its cosmetic and traditional uses to be small,[8] and the TikTok-focused papers examine what online creators claim rather than hair outcomes.[7][8]

Rice water is discussed as a low-cost home remedy next to products such as minoxidil. A T Nation forum user wrote that people were 'all over' fermented rice water while naming minoxidil and Monistat shampoo as the products they considered known to work.[3] In hair-length and hair-quality discussions it is usually presented as a conditioning step rather than a loss treatment.

Rice water travelled from family and regional practice into global beauty culture through K-beauty content, hair-growth forums and short video. The TikTok cross-sectional analysis in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery is a published attempt to characterise that content, and a 2023 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology paper on 'hairfluencer' trends was written to brief dermatologists on topics patients raise after seeing them online.[7][8] The Cutis review frames patients as increasingly taking hair-loss advice from social media rather than from clinicians.[8]

timeline.event: Heian period in Japan, during which women are reported to have washed their hair in rice water.[2]
A Lancet report on rice water for infantile gastroenteritis, part of the food and medical history of rice water.[2]
A systematic review of rice-derived hair products, mainly rice bran extracts, is described as reporting possible strength and breakage benefits.[1]
A Cutis review examines rice water and other topical hair-loss remedies promoted on TikTok.[8]
A systematic review in the Journal of Food Science and Technology surveys uses of rice-washed water and calls for scientific validation.[8]
A cross-sectional analysis of rice water for hair and skin on TikTok appears in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery.[7]

lore.intro: Rice water is discussed in beauty and hair-growth circles as a traditional remedy, frequently linked to the long hair of Yao women in Huangluo and to the K-beauty trend.[1][3]

claims.claim: Fermented rice water makes hair grow longer.
claims.believers: Proponents point to traditions such as the Yao women of Huangluo and to personal results from regular rinses.[1]
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports that strong scientific evidence for increased hair length or growth rate is lacking and describes claims as anecdotal.[1]

claims.claim: Rice water strengthens hair and reduces breakage.
claims.believers: Supporters credit inositol and amino acids for elasticity and friction reduction.[1]
claims.experts: Grokipedia says a 2022 review of small trials suggested possible benefits for hair strength and breakage, but mostly with rice bran products rather than rice water.[1]

claims.claim: Rice water is a hair-growth rival to minoxidil.
claims.believers: A T Nation user observed the trend but ranked minoxidil and Monistat shampoo above it.[3]
claims.experts: Minoxidil is an approved hair-growth treatment; no published trials have compared rice water to it.

claims.claim: Rice water leaves hair smoother and shinier.
claims.believers: Users describe softer, less tangled hair after rinses, crediting starches and lipids.[1]
claims.experts: Grokipedia notes that protein buildup can instead make hair stiff or brittle in some hair types.[1]

claims.claim: Rice water is what keeps the Yao women of Huangluo's hair so long
claims.believers: Popular media and the women themselves attribute their very long hair to regular fermented rice rinses.[1]
claims.experts: No published study has tested rice water on hair length in that community or elsewhere.

claims.claim: Social-media rice water routines are an established hair-growth remedy
claims.believers: Creators present rice water as a natural route to longer, thicker hair.[7]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviewers describe such trends as popular online and examine the supporting evidence, which the Cutis review lists among herbs and extracts with limited trial data.[8]
